newsitem.title: UK: Thwarted IRA brings war home to Northern Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Thwarted IRA brings war home to Northern Ireland.

text.p: The IRA decided to bring its war back home to Northern Ireland with a bomb attack on army headquarters after its plans for "spectaculars" on mainland Britain were foiled by police, security analysts said on Thursday.

A double car bomb attack that wounded 31 people and blew a crater in the heart of Britain's chief army garrrison at Lisburn on Monday also torpedoed hopes of a truce before next year's British election, they said.
The bombing, one of the Irish Republican Army's (IRA) most audacious in a long and bloody war against British rule, was its first in the province for two years.
Since ditching a 17-month ceasefire in February, the guerrilla group has set off a string of bombs in British cities, and one at a military base in Germany.

But British security sources said recent breakthroughs by mainland police had thwarted plans for the type of headline-grabbing attack the guerrillas had hoped would force Britain to make concessions to its Sinn Fein political wing.

British anti-terrorist police arrested five IRA suspects and killed another in a raid in London late last month, which snared 10 tonnes of explosives and several weapons. It was the latest in a series of coups against the IRA's network in England.
"It's easier to undertake offensive action in Northern Ireland because they don't have the same logistical problems as they do on the mainland," said a British security expert.
"They would have preferred, in an ideal situation, to bomb the mainland and not to have to resort to bombing in Northern Ireland. They have now resorted to the easier option."
The Lisburn bomb shattered Anglo-Irish efforts to establish a permament peace through multi-party talks and brought the province to the brink of renewed sectarian conflict.

Pro-British Loyalist guerrillas are reported to have met secretly since Monday to decide whether to retaliate by ditching their two-year ceasefire and plunging the region into a new cycle of sectarian warfare.
"I very much doubt that there is going to be a ceasefire this side of the general election," said Henry Patterson, professor of politics at the University of Ulster.
Patterson said he believed the leaders of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, were taken by surprise by the Lisburn bombing and would have opposed it.
The attack highlighted divisions within the republican movement over whether to seek progress through negotiation or to carry on with the armed struggle, he said.

Patterson believed the guerrillas have given up on current multi-party talks in the hope that the British general election, due by next May, will bring in a Labour government ready to offer new peace initiatives.
The IRA said it abandoned its last ceasefire because of the Conservative government's refusal to relax demands that the guerrillas give up their arms before Sinn Fein is allowed into the peace talks.
Republicans accuse the government of being reluctant to break new ground because with a majority of only one, it needs to keep the support of Protestant Unionist members of parliament.

"I think ultimately the IRA would have preferred to try to maintain a de facto ceasefire up until the election and then get into a bargaining situation," Patterson said. Margaret O'Callaghan, politics lecturer at Queen's University Belfast, agreed: "The Lisburn bombing very seriously damages prospects of a ceasefire or any prospect of Sinn Fein going into talks," she said.
